newsitem.title: GERMANY: Welteke-Talk of EMU delay hurts German economy.
newsitem.headline: Welteke-Talk of EMU delay hurts German economy.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke said on Monday that talk of delaying Europe's planned monetary union was negative (EMU) and would only hurt the Germany economy and worsen its unemployment levels.

In the introduction to the annual report for the State Central Bank of Hessen, Welteke also said the euro would not be a weak currency and would be more stable than the deutschemark against non-EMU currencies duch as the yen and the dollar.
"The discussion about delaying the euro's introduction should be judged as negative. A delay would help neither the German economy nor its workers," Welteke wrote.
He said talk of delay was all the more damaging to Germany's economic recovery, since it led to jitters in financial markets and a flow of funds into the mark.

The Bundesbank official said the impending currency union would not solve the European Union's (EU) unemployment problems, since they were largely due to structural causes, but would improve prospects for economic growth and job creation.
"(EMU) is therefore not only in the interests of the Germany economy but also in those of its workers," he wrote.
He said the disappearance of foreign exchange fluctuations within the euro-area would help long-term export strategies and improve conditions for investment.
"This will bring considerable advantages for Germany," he said, adding that in the past, the German export sector had been particularly successful in periods of sustained currency stability.

Looking at the Maastricht convergence rules for the union, Welteke said the fiscal criteria -- which include a call for members to bring their debt to gross domestic product ration to three percent or below -- left room for interpretation.
He said too much emphasis was being placed on the strict 3.0 percent goal in Germany's debate over the euro.

Numerous German politicians have repeatedly said Germany will meet its aim of a 2.9 percent deficit/GDP ratio in 1997, but many independent economists say cripplingly high unemployment will prevent the government hitting that goal.
Welteke said the euro's introduction should not be blamed for a current lack of scope for domestic economic expansion, saying the "sins of the past" were far more to blame.
He said state debt had reached a point at which it was becoming a "deficit trap", with 16 percent of tax income going straight into debt servicing payments.
Fiscal discipline and not more spending, was the key to economic growth.

"Solid fiscal policy creates confidence on financial markets, draws in capital and contributes to lower interest rates," Welteke said. "And greater confidence and a better economic climate encourage investment."
